# Interpreting This Plot

## What It Shows

This is a line graph of **average annual global temperature in Fahrenheit from 1880 to 2015**. The y-axis spans from roughly -10°F to 110°F, while the data line hovers in a narrow band around **55–58°F** across the entire 135-year period.

## The Apparent Message

At first glance, the line looks almost perfectly flat — suggesting global temperature has been essentially unchanged for over a century.

## Why That Impression Is Misleading

This is a classic example of how **axis scaling shapes interpretation**:

- **The y-axis range is vastly oversized** for the data. By stretching the vertical axis across 120 degrees when the actual variation is only about 2–3 degrees, any real change gets visually compressed into near-invisibility.
- **Each gridline represents 5°F**, so a change of 2°F — climatologically enormous — barely registers as a line thickness.
- If the y-axis were rescaled to, say, 55–59°F, the same data would show a clearly visible **upward trend**, particularly accelerating after about 1970.

## What's Actually in the Data

Looking closely, you *can* detect:
- Slightly cooler values around 1900–1915
- A gradual rise mid-century
- A noticeable uptick from the 1980s onward, with the line sitting visibly higher by 2010–2015 than at any earlier point

## The Takeaway

The underlying data is consistent with the scientific record of roughly **1.5–2°F of global warming since 1880**. The graph doesn't falsify data — it simply presents it at a scale that obscures the trend. It's a useful teaching example of how a technically accurate chart can still lead viewers toward a misleading conclusion.

A better version would either narrow the y-axis to the relevant range or plot **temperature anomalies** (deviations from a baseline average), which is the standard convention in climate science precisely because it makes meaningful changes visible.

The chart plots average annual global temperature (°F) from 1880 to about 2010. The line sits near 57–58°F the whole time and looks almost flat, with only a slight rise toward the right that is hard to see.

That flat appearance is mostly an artifact of the scale. The y-axis runs from −10 to 110, a span of 120 degrees, while the real change in global mean temperature over this period is only on the order of 1–2°F. On a range that wide, a scientifically meaningful warming trend is compressed into a nearly horizontal line. A plot of temperature anomaly (departure from a baseline), or the same series with a y-axis zoomed to the actual range of the data, would show the rise clearly.

## What's literally on the chart

Two normal (Gaussian) curves, both with SD = 15, centered at 100 and 85. This isn't data — it's a schematic drawing of two idealized distributions from two parameters each. There's no sample, no error bars, and the y-axis has no units.

## Reading the geometry

The gap is exactly 1 SD (d = 1.0). A few things follow mechanically:

- **Large overlap.** The shared area is about 62% of each distribution. The curves are far more alike than different.
- **Group means predict individuals poorly.** If you drew one person at random from each curve, the person from the lower-mean group would score higher roughly **24%** of the time. Knowing someone's group membership explains about 20% of the variance in this model — most variation is *within* groups, not between.
- **Tails amplify.** Small mean shifts produce big ratios far from center. Above 130, the blue curve has ~2.3% and the orange ~0.13% — a ~17:1 ratio. This is why such charts are often deployed to argue about elite outcomes, and it's also where the model's assumptions (perfect normality out to 3 SD) are least trustworthy.

## What the chart doesn't show, and should

**The numbers are dated.** The 85 figure reflects test data largely from the 1960s–80s. The gap has narrowed since: analyses of NAEP, NLSY, and standardization samples (e.g., Dickens & Flynn 2006) put the convergence at roughly a third to a half of a standard deviation over several decades. A static 1994 snapshot presented as a timeless distribution hides that trend — and a gap that moves on a generational timescale is hard to attribute to anything fixed.

**The Flynn effect dwarfs the gap.** Raw IQ performance rose roughly 3 points per decade through the 20th century — a full standard deviation in about 30 years, purely environmental. Whatever moved scores that much can plausibly account for a 15-point group difference.

**The chart embeds a causal claim in its title.** "By race" frames race as the explanatory variable. But race is a social classification, not a natural kind with crisp genetic boundaries, and it is tightly confounded with school quality, family wealth, neighborhood segregation, lead and other toxic exposures, nutrition, healthcare access, and test familiarity. A plot "IQ by childhood household income" would look similar and would not tempt anyone to conclude income is genetic.

**Within-group heritability ≠ between-group heritability.** This is the central logical error in hereditarian readings of *The Bell Curve*. Height is highly heritable within populations, yet mean height differences between cohorts came mostly from nutrition. Lewontin's seed analogy: identical seeds in rich vs. poor soil produce two distributions with a mean gap that is 0% genetic, even though variation within each pot is ~100% genetic.

**The expert consensus is explicitly agnostic.** The APA's task force report *Intelligence: Knowns and Unknowns* (Neisser et al., 1996), convened partly in response to this book, concluded that the gap is real on these tests, is not attributable to test bias in the technical psychometric sense, and has **no adequate explanation** — with no direct evidence supporting a genetic one. That remains roughly the state of the field.

## Bottom line

As a visualization, it's an accurate rendering of two normal curves one SD apart. As an argument, it does a lot of work through omission: it presents a model as data, freezes a moving quantity, and uses the title to imply a cause the plot can't test. If you encounter this chart in the wild, the useful questions are *whose data, from what year, and compared to what alternative explanatory variable?*

# Interpreting the Chart: "Top 5 Counties with the Greatest Number of Confirmed COVID-19 Cases"

## What the Visualization Shows

This is a **grouped (clustered) bar chart** displaying daily confirmed COVID-19 case counts across five Georgia counties — **Cobb, DeKalb, Fulton, Gwinnett, and Hall** — over a 15-day window spanning late April through early May 2020. Each date on the x-axis has a cluster of up to five colored bars, one per county, with the y-axis measuring new confirmed cases (ranging roughly 0–170).

## Key Observations

**1. The dates are sorted by magnitude, not chronology.**
This is the most important structural feature. Reading left to right, the x-axis goes 28Apr → 27Apr → 29Apr → 01May → 30Apr → 04May → 06May → 05May → 02May → 07May → 26Apr → 03May → 08May → 09May. The chart appears sorted in **descending order of total (or maximum) daily cases**, so the downward slope is *not* an epidemiological trend — it's an artifact of the sort order.

**2. One dramatic outlier dominates.**
Hall County (teal) on 28Apr2020 shows roughly **167 cases** — far above any other single bar. This is consistent with a localized outbreak cluster (Hall County experienced well-documented poultry-processing plant outbreaks in spring 2020). Notably, Hall's values collapse quickly on most other dates, appearing in the 25–30 range or lower.

**3. Highest-volume days cluster in late April.**
Fulton County peaks around **108 cases on 29Apr**, Cobb around **95 on 27Apr**, and 28Apr/27Apr both show multiple counties in the 60–90 range. The bars with the smallest values — 08May, 09May, and 03May — sit at the right end.

**4. Recent dates show very low counts — likely reporting lag.**
The final clusters (08May, 09May) show near-zero bars for most counties. Rather than indicating the epidemic ended, this almost certainly reflects **incomplete reporting**: cases from the most recent days hadn't yet been confirmed and entered into the system at the time this snapshot was generated.

**5. Fulton and Cobb are the most consistent contributors.**
Across the mid-range dates, Fulton (yellow/gold) and Cobb (purple) regularly post among the highest counts, which aligns with their large populations in metro Atlanta.

## Caveats and Limitations

- **Raw counts, not rates.** Without population normalization (cases per 100,000), larger counties naturally appear worse. Hall County is much smaller than Fulton or Gwinnett, so its 167-case day is proportionally far more severe than the chart alone conveys.
- **The sort order is misleading.** A viewer skimming this chart would likely read the left-to-right decline as "cases are falling," which the data does not support. Re-plotting chronologically — ideally as a multi-series line chart with a 7-day rolling average — would communicate the actual trend far more honestly.
- **Missing bars are ambiguous.** Some clusters show fewer than five bars; it's unclear whether those represent zero cases or missing data.
- **No denominator for testing.** Confirmed cases depend heavily on testing volume, which varied considerably during this period.

## Suggested Improvements

Plot dates chronologically on the x-axis, switch to lines or a stacked area chart to reduce visual clutter from 75 individual bars, add a rolling average to smooth day-of-week reporting effects, normalize by population, and shade or annotate the most recent days to flag incomplete reporting.

Group means of this kind also do not identify any individual’s score, and the causes of average test-score differences—environment, schooling, health, socioeconomic conditions, test design, and other factors—are not shown by the figure and remain disputed.

# Interpreting This Plot

## What's Shown
This is a line graph titled **"Average Annual Global Temperature in Fahrenheit, 1880–2015."** The x-axis spans roughly 135 years in 10-year increments, and the y-axis runs from about **-10°F to 110°F** in 5-degree steps.

## The Apparent Message
At first glance, the orange line looks almost perfectly **flat**, hovering around **57–58°F** across the entire period. A casual viewer would conclude that global temperature has been essentially unchanged for over a century.

## The Catch: Misleading Axis Scaling
This is a classic example of how **axis choice can distort interpretation**:

- The y-axis covers a **120-degree range**, while the actual data varies by only about **2°F** over the full record.
- That real variation gets compressed into roughly **1–2% of the chart's vertical space**, making a genuine trend visually invisible.
- The data are displayed as **absolute temperatures** rather than **anomalies** (deviations from a baseline), which is how climate scientists normally present this information precisely because anomalies reveal change more reliably.

## What the Data Actually Show
If you look very closely, the line does tick upward — slightly lower values around 1900–1915, a gentle rise mid-century, and a visible uptick after about 1980 toward the right edge. Published records (NASA GISS, NOAA) show roughly **+1.8°F (1.0°C) of warming** from 1880 to 2015, with most of it since 1970.

## Takeaway
The plot is **technically accurate but rhetorically misleading**. It's often used to argue that climate change is negligible. The appropriate rebuttal: a 2°F global average shift is enormous in climate terms — the difference between today and the last ice age is only about 9°F — and the chart's scale, not the data, is what hides it.

**Better practice:** plot temperature anomalies on a y-axis scaled to the actual range of variation (e.g., -1.5°F to +2.0°F), and add a trend line or smoothed average.

**Two factors narrow the gap rather than widen it.** Education contributes −5.9%, meaning women's educational attainment is on average higher and, all else equal, would push their wages *above* men's. The chart's footnote stresses these are estimates, and the boundaries between categories are not clean. Discrimination may itself drive occupational segregation (so the "occupation" share partly embeds discrimination), while the "unexplained" share may include genuine productivity differences that simply aren't observed in the data. The decomposition is therefore best read as an indicative accounting rather than a precise causal attribution.

## What the plot literally shows

Two idealized normal distributions, both with SD = 15, with means set 15 points (1 SD) apart — 100 and 85. These are the summary parameters Herrnstein and Murray used in *The Bell Curve* (1994) to describe the average Black–White gap on IQ tests in U.S. samples of that era.

A few things follow mathematically from that setup:

- **Large overlap.** The overlap area of the two curves is about 62%. Pick a random person from each group and the Black individual scores higher roughly 24% of the time.
- **Within-group variation dwarfs the between-group difference.** The full width of each curve spans ~80 points; the gap between the means is 15.
- **Tails diverge sharply.** A 1-SD mean shift has a modest effect near the center but a large proportional effect at the extremes. Above 130, the curves imply ~2.3% vs. ~0.1% — a ratio of roughly 17:1. This is a generic property of shifted normals, not a special fact about IQ.
- **Zero individual predictive value.** Knowing which curve someone was drawn from tells you almost nothing about that person's score.

## What the plot does *not* show

- **Causation.** A distribution plot is purely descriptive. It cannot distinguish genetic, environmental, educational, socioeconomic, nutritional, or measurement-related explanations. The data are identical under all of them.
- **Fixedness.** The gap is not a constant. Analyses by Dickens and Flynn (2006) and others found it narrowed by roughly 4–7 points between the 1970s and 2000s. - **Accurate distributional shape.** The real distributions aren't perfectly matched normals. Reported SDs for Black samples are often somewhat smaller (~12–13), and both distributions show deviations in the tails.
- **A well-defined grouping variable.** "Race" here is a self-reported social category in U.S. survey data, strongly confounded with income, school quality, residential segregation, lead exposure, healthcare access, and test familiarity. It is not a clean biological partition.

## Context on the source

*The Bell Curve* was heavily criticized on methodological grounds — the APA's 1996 task force report *Intelligence: Knowns and Unknowns* accepted the existence of the score gap but concluded there was no adequate explanation for it and specifically no direct evidence for a genetic contribution. Critics also noted the book leaned on a narrow and ideologically selective literature for its race chapters.

This is a correct rendering of a well-replicated *measurement* finding, presented in a way that visually emphasizes the mean difference. The honest reading is: group averages on these tests differed by about a standard deviation in 1990s U.S. data, the distributions overlap substantially, the gap has shrunk over time, and the chart itself is silent on why.

**The numbers aren't fixed.** The Black–white gap in the U.S. has narrowed substantially since the 1970s, by roughly a third on several measures. Separately, the Flynn effect raised raw scores ~3 points per decade across populations through the 20th century — enough that a 1940s white mean would fall near the 1990s Black mean. Gaps that move this fast are hard to attribute to fixed causes.

**"Race" here is a social category.** The groupings are self-identified census categories, not genetically discrete populations; human genetic variation is mostly continuous and mostly within rather than between such groups.

**Ecological fallacy risk.** Charts like this invite reasoning from group mean to individual expectation. That inference is statistically invalid given the overlap shown — the plot's own geometry argues against the use it is often put to.

## Bottom line

The figure accurately depicts a one-SD separation between two assumed distributions, with heavy overlap and amplified divergence in the tails. It documents a measured disparity in test performance from a particular era. It does not — and cannot — show what produced that disparity, and the visual drama of two separated peaks tends to overstate how much the distinction tells you about any given person.

# Interpreting This Chart

## What's shown
This is a line graph titled **"Average Annual Global Temperature in Fahrenheit, 1880–2015."** The horizontal axis spans roughly 135 years in 10-year increments; the vertical axis runs from −10°F to 110°F in 5-degree steps.

## What the data appears to say
The orange line sits flat at roughly **56–58°F** across the entire period. At this scale, the line looks essentially horizontal — suggesting global temperature has been virtually unchanged since 1880.

## Why that impression is misleading
This is a classic example of how **axis scaling can distort a story**:

- **The y-axis is vastly over-extended.** The actual data occupy a band of maybe 2°F, but the axis covers 120°F. Over 98% of the plot area is empty space, compressing all real variation into a thin line.
- **Real global warming of ~1.5–2°F (roughly 1°C) since 1880 is genuine and climatologically significant** — it's the difference between stable ice sheets and widespread melt — but it's invisible when plotted against a range that would accommodate the temperature swing between a freezing night and a desert afternoon.
- **A faint upward tilt is still detectable**, with the line appearing slightly lower around 1900–1920 and slightly higher after about 1980, hinting at the warming trend buried in the scale.

## A better presentation
Plotting a y-axis of roughly **55–59°F**, or showing **anomalies** (departures from a baseline average) — the convention climate scientists actually use — would make the trend and year-to-year variability legible.

## Takeaway
The chart's data are presumably accurate, but the visual design suppresses the signal. It's a useful lesson that **"the line looks flat" is a statement about the chart, not necessarily about the world.** Whenever most of a graph is blank space, ask whether the axis range was chosen to illuminate the data — or to bury it.

## What the plot shows mechanically

Two idealized normal (Gaussian) curves, both with SD = 15, centered 15 points apart — exactly one standard deviation. Everything in the figure follows from those two numbers:

- **Overlap:** roughly 62% of the two distributions coincide. The shaded gray region dominates the picture.
- **Rank probability:** if you drew one person at random from each curve, the person from the lower-mean curve would score higher about **24%** of the time.
- **Crossover:** the curves intersect at IQ ≈ 92.5, the midpoint.
- **Above 100:** 50% of one group vs. ~16% of the other.
- **Tails:** a 1-SD shift has disproportionate effects at the extremes. Above 130, you'd expect ~2.3% vs. ~0.13% — a ~17× ratio. This is a general mathematical property of shifted normals, not a special fact about IQ.

The single most important feature visually is that **the within-group spread is much larger than the between-group gap.** Knowing which curve someone was drawn from tells you very little about that individual.

## What the plot is not

**It isn't data.** These are smooth analytic curves generated from two parameters. There are no sample sizes, confidence intervals, years, or sampling frames. Real score distributions are not perfectly normal and don't have identical SDs.

**The parameters are dated and contested.** The 85/100 figures come from *The Bell Curve* (1994), drawing largely on the NLSY79 and older test batteries. Most subsequent analyses find the Black–White gap on US cognitive tests has narrowed — commonly estimated at ~0.6–0.8 SD in more recent cohorts, with larger convergence among younger test-takers. A chart labeled with 1994 means presented without a date caveat implies a fixed quantity that is in fact moving.

**It describes test scores, not "intelligence" as a property of groups.** The curves summarize performance on particular instruments, in particular populations, at particular times. "White" and "Black" here are US social categories, not biologically discrete populations; genetic variation is overwhelmingly within rather than between such categories.

## The interpretive trap

The chart is purely descriptive, but its framing — race as the organizing variable, no other covariates — invites a causal reading it cannot support. Measured gaps of this kind covary heavily with factors that differ sharply across these groups in the US: family and neighborhood income, school quality and funding, parental education, segregation history, prenatal and childhood health, lead exposure, and test-taking context.

Two points are worth stating explicitly because they're frequently confused:

1. **Within-group heritability says nothing about between-group causes.** Height is highly heritable within populations, yet mean height differences between cohorts have been driven by nutrition. Richard Lewontin's standard illustration: identical seed mixes grown in rich vs. poor soil produce heritable variation within each tray and an entirely environmental difference between trays.

2. **The Flynn effect dwarfs the gap.** Raw IQ performance rose roughly 3 points per decade across the 20th century in many countries — meaning the within-century environmental shift exceeded the gap shown here. That demonstrates these distributions are highly movable by non-genetic factors.

The APA's 1996 task force report (*Intelligence: Knowns and Unknowns*), convened partly in response to *The Bell Curve*, concluded that the gap was real as measured, not attributable simply to test bias in the narrow psychometric sense, and **not explained** — with no direct empirical support for a genetic account. That remains the mainstream position in the field.

## Bottom line

As a statistics exercise, the figure correctly illustrates how two distributions separated by 1 SD relate — especially the large overlap and the amplified tail ratios. As a claim about the world, it's a schematic of a dated, heavily-debated estimate, stripped of the sampling, temporal, and causal context needed to interpret it. If you're using it for anything beyond illustrating properties of normal curves, those caveats should be on the chart.

## What the chart shows

This is a horizontal bar chart from Our World in Data (source: Blau and Kahn, 2017) that breaks down the total gender wage gap into the fractions attributable to different labor-market variables. Bars extend right of zero for factors that *widen* the gap and left of zero for factors that *narrow* it.

## The values, ranked

| Factor | Share of the gap |
|---|---|
| Unexplained | 38% |
| Occupation | 32.9% |
| Industry | 17.6% |
| Experience | 14.1% |
| Race | 4.3% |
| Region | 0.3% |
| Unionization | −1.3% |
| Education | −5.9% |

## Interpretation

**The single largest component is "unexplained" (38%).** This is the residual left over once all observable factors are accounted for, and it is often read as a proxy for discrimination — though the chart's own note cautions it may also capture unobserved differences (e.g., in productivity).

**Occupational and industrial segregation together dominate the explained portion.** Occupation (32.9%) and industry (17.6%) sum to just over half the gap, indicating that *where* men and women work — which jobs and which sectors — matters far more than most other measured characteristics.

**Experience still contributes meaningfully (14.1%),** reflecting differences in accumulated years in the labor force, often tied to career interruptions around childbearing and caregiving.

**Education now works in women's favor (−5.9%).** The negative sign means that, on average, women's educational attainment is high enough that it *reduces* the gap; if education were the only factor, women would earn more. Unionization is also mildly gap-narrowing (−1.3%). Region is essentially negligible (0.3%).

## Caveats worth stressing

The decomposition is an estimate, and the categories are not cleanly separable. Discrimination can itself drive occupational segregation, meaning some of what is labeled "occupation" may really be discrimination operating upstream. Conversely, part of the "unexplained" share may reflect genuine unmeasured differences rather than bias. The boundaries between bars should therefore be treated as analytically convenient rather than causally precise.

# Interpreting This Plot

## What's shown
This is a line graph titled **"Average Annual Global Temperature in Fahrenheit, 1880–2015."** The x-axis spans roughly 135 years (1880 to about 2015, marked in decades), and the y-axis runs from –10°F to 110°F in 5-degree increments.

## The apparent message
At first glance, the orange line looks almost perfectly **flat**, hovering right around 57–58°F for the entire period. The visual impression is that global temperature has essentially **not changed at all** over 135 years.

## Why that impression is misleading
This is a classic example of how **axis scaling can distort interpretation**:

- **The y-axis range is far too wide.** Actual global temperature variation over this period is roughly 1.5–2°F. Compressed into a 120-degree axis, that real change becomes a line thickness — visually invisible.
- **The scale is irrelevant to the data.** No annual global average has ever been near –10°F or 110°F, so about 98% of the plot area is empty space that serves no purpose except to flatten the signal.
- **A proper chart** of this same data — with a y-axis spanning, say, 56°F to 59°F — would show a clear, pronounced upward trend, especially a steep rise from about 1970 onward.

## What's actually in the data
Looking very closely, the line does show subtle features consistent with the real record: a slight dip around 1900–1910, a modest rise through the 1940s, a plateau mid-century, and a visible uptick at the right-hand end (post-1980), where the line sits noticeably higher than at the left.

## Takeaway
The underlying data likely reflect genuine global warming, but **this presentation obscures rather than reveals it.** Whether intentional or not, the chart demonstrates why you should always check the y-axis before drawing conclusions from a line graph — a "flat" line can be an artifact of the scale, not a finding about the world.

## What the plot literally shows

Two idealized normal (Gaussian) curves, each with a standard deviation of 15, with means set 15 points apart (100 and 85) — the figures popularized by Herrnstein and Murray's *The Bell Curve* (1994). The dashed vertical lines mark the two means.

Some quantitative features worth reading off:

- **The separation is exactly 1 SD** (Cohen's *d* = 1.0). That's a large effect by social-science conventions.
- **The overlap is large.** Two normals one SD apart share roughly 62% of their area. The shaded region where both curves are substantial spans most of the plot.
- **Implied tail asymmetries:** about 16% of the lower-mean distribution falls above 100, and about 84% of the higher-mean distribution falls above 85. Differences compound in the tails — at 130+, the ratio of densities is large even though absolute numbers are small in both groups.

## Important caveats about what it doesn't show

**It's a model, not data.** These are smooth theoretical curves, not histograms of observed scores. There are no sample sizes, no confidence intervals, no indication of which tests, which cohorts, or which years. Real score distributions are not exactly normal and the means are sample estimates that vary by test and sample.

**The numbers are dated and the gap is not fixed.** The 85/100 figures reflect mid-20th-century test data. Analyses by Dickens and Flynn and others find the Black–White gap narrowed by roughly 0.2–0.3 SD between the 1970s and 2000s. More strikingly, the Flynn effect — secular IQ gains of roughly 3 points per decade across the 20th century — means that entire populations shifted by more than this gap within a few generations. Whatever moves population means around, it works fast, which is hard to square with a fixed, immutable difference.

**A gap is a measurement, not an explanation.** The plot shows a difference in test scores. It says nothing about why. Candidate causes that are well-documented include differences in school quality and funding, family wealth (which is far more unequal than income), lead and other environmental exposures, nutrition, health care access, and the direct and compounding effects of a long history of legal discrimination. Hereditarian explanations for the *between-group* portion of the gap remain unsupported — within-group heritability of a trait tells you nothing about the source of between-group differences (the standard illustration: genetically identical seed stock grown in rich vs. poor soil yields a fully "heritable" height difference between plots that is entirely environmental).

**"Race" is a poor partition for biological inference.** Racial categories are social and administrative classifications with shifting boundaries; most human genetic variation is within these groups rather than between them.

**The individual-level inference is near-worthless.** This is the most common misuse of a chart like this. Group membership explains a tiny fraction of the variance in any individual's score. Given the overlap shown, knowing someone's racial category tells you very little about their cognitive test performance — and nothing about any individual you could instead simply test, interview, or evaluate directly.

## A note on the framing

The visualization makes a rhetorical choice: it foregrounds the two mean lines and the gap between them. A chart emphasizing the ~62% overlap, or one plotting each group's within-group spread against the between-group difference, would convey the same data with a very different impression. Charts like this circulate widely in contexts arguing for innate group differences; the statistics displayed do not support that conclusion, and the visual design does some persuasive work that the underlying numbers don't.

# Interpretation of the Plot

## What's Shown
This line graph displays **average annual global temperature in degrees Fahrenheit from 1880 to 2015**. The orange line hovers consistently around the **55–58°F** range across the entire 135-year period, appearing almost perfectly flat.

## The Key Issue: Misleading Y-Axis Scale

The most important thing to notice about this chart is that the **y-axis spans from -10°F to 110°F** — a range of 120 degrees. Meanwhile, the actual variation in global average temperature over this period is roughly **2°F**.

Because the data occupies less than 2% of the vertical space available, the warming trend is visually compressed into what looks like a straight horizontal line. A casual viewer might conclude that global temperature has been essentially unchanged since 1880.

## What the Data Actually Shows

If you look carefully, there *is* a subtle upward tilt, particularly after about 1980 — the line sits slightly higher on the right side than the left. On a properly scaled axis (say, 56°F to 59°F), this same data would reveal a pronounced warming trend, especially the sharp rise in recent decades.

## Takeaway

This is a classic example of how **axis scaling can shape perception without altering a single data point**. The chart is technically accurate but rhetorically deceptive. Whether intentional or not, it minimizes a change that is scientifically significant — a 2°F shift in global mean temperature represents an enormous amount of accumulated energy in the climate system.

**Lesson for reading charts:** Always check the axis range first. Ask whether the scale is appropriate to the magnitude of variation in the data, or whether it has been stretched/compressed to make a trend look bigger or smaller than it is.

The chart shows average annual global temperature from 1880 to 2015. The orange line stays around 57–59°F across the full period, with a slight upward drift. Because the y-axis spans roughly -10°F to 110°F, that small change appears nearly flat.

## What the figure literally shows

Two idealized normal (Gaussian) curves, not actual data — just the math implied by two parameters each: a mean and SD of 15. The only real "information content" is the 15-point (1 SD) separation between the means.

A few quantities you can read off directly:

- **Overlap:** the shaded common area is about 62% of each distribution. These are not two separate populations; they are two heavily overlapping ones.
- **Rank comparison:** pick one person at random from each curve, and the person from the lower-mean distribution scores higher about 24% of the time.
- **Tails amplify:** a 1 SD mean difference has modest effects near the middle but large *ratio* effects far out. Above 130, the blue curve has roughly 17× the density; below 70, the orange curve has roughly 7×. This tail-amplification property is the figure's main rhetorical punch, and it is a generic feature of any two shifted normals — it would look the same for height distributions of two arbitrary groups.

## What the figure does not show

**It's descriptive, not causal.** A gap in average test scores is an observation. The plot contains zero information about *why* the means differ. Shifting a distribution's mean is something environments do routinely and powerfully.

**The Flynn effect is the key scale reference.** Measured IQ rose roughly 3 points per decade through the 20th century in dozens of countries. That means environmental/secular factors moved whole national distributions by *more than 15 points* within a couple of generations. Whatever caused that is big enough to cause a gap this size.

**The numbers are dated.** The 85 figure comes from mid-20th-century US samples. The Black–White gap in the US has narrowed by roughly 4–7 points since the 1970s on several national datasets (Dickens & Flynn 2006), with most of the convergence among younger cohorts. A static 1994 snapshot presented as a fixed property of populations misrepresents a moving quantity.

**Equal SDs are an assumption.** Several US samples show a somewhat smaller SD (~12–13) for the lower-mean group, which changes the tail ratios the plot implies.

**Within-group heritability ≠ between-group heritability.** This is the central logical error in hereditarian readings of such plots. Lewontin's illustration: plant genetically varied seed in two pots, one with poor soil. Height differences *within* each pot are highly heritable; the difference *between* pots is entirely environmental. The Bell Curve's own inference from high within-group heritability to a genetic between-group cause doesn't follow.

**"Race" here is self-identified social category**, not a genetic partition. African American populations have substantial and variable European admixture, and admixture studies have not found the score–ancestry correlations a genetic hypothesis predicts.

**Confounds are not controlled.** The groups differ systematically in school funding and quality, parental wealth (a far larger gap than income), childhood lead and other toxin exposure, nutrition, healthcare access, incarceration exposure, and test familiarity — plus a documented history of segregation whose effects persist across generations.

## How it was received

The APA's post-*Bell Curve* task force (Neisser et al., 1996) — a deliberately balanced panel — concluded that the gap was real in the test data, that it was not attributable to test bias in the narrow psychometric sense, and that **there was no adequate explanation for it and no direct evidence supporting a genetic one**. That remains roughly the mainstream position, with the added evidence of convergence since.

## The individual-level point

With 62% overlap, group membership is close to worthless for predicting any individual's score — the within-group variance dwarfs the between-group difference. A plot like this is sometimes used to justify inferences about individuals; the geometry of the plot itself refutes that use.

## Bottom line

As a visualization, it's an honest rendering of two parameters. As an argument, it's underdetermined: it shows a *difference in measured means* and invites the viewer to supply a cause. The scientific literature doesn't supply one, the gap has been shrinking, and comparable or larger shifts are known to be environmentally producible.

# Interpreting This Plot

## What's Shown
This line graph displays **average annual global temperature in Fahrenheit from 1880 to 2015**. The orange line hovers steadily around 57–58°F across the entire 135-year span, appearing almost perfectly flat.

## The Critical Issue: Misleading Y-Axis Scaling

This chart is a textbook example of how **axis choices can obscure real data**. The y-axis runs from –10°F to 110°F — a 120-degree range — while the actual variation in global average temperature over this period is roughly **1.5–2°F**.

Because the data occupies less than 2% of the vertical space, genuine warming is compressed into what looks like a straight line.

## What's Actually in the Data

Looking closely, subtle features are still visible:
- A slight **dip around 1900–1915** (cooler early-century period)
- A gentle **rise from the 1920s–1940s**
- A **plateau mid-century** (1940s–1970s)
- A **visible upward tick from roughly 1980 onward**, with the line ending noticeably higher than it began

These match the well-documented historical temperature record, where global averages rose about 1.8°F (1.0°C) since the late 19th century.

## The Takeaway

**Scale matters.** A chart like this could be used — intentionally or not — to argue that global temperature "hasn't really changed." But choosing a 120-degree axis for data that varies by under 2 degrees is like measuring a person's height change with a scale that spans from ground level to the top of a building.

A more informative version would use a y-axis spanning roughly 56–59°F, or plot **temperature anomalies** (deviations from a baseline average) — the standard approach in climate science, precisely because it makes meaningful variation visible.

**Context for why small numbers matter:** A 2°F global average shift is enormous in climate terms. The difference between today and the depths of the last ice age is only about 11°F.

## What the plot literally shows

Two idealized normal (Gaussian) curves, not actual data. Each is drawn with SD = 15 and a mean taken from *The Bell Curve* (Herrnstein & Murray, 1994): 100 and 85. The dashed vertical lines mark the means; the shaded regions are just the areas under each curve. Because both curves use the same SD and the same assumed shape, the picture contains essentially two numbers — a 15-point difference, which is exactly one standard deviation (Cohen's *d* = 1.0).

## What follows arithmetically from that assumption

- **Overlap is large.** Roughly 62% of the two distributions overlap. If you drew one person at random from each group, the person from the lower-mean distribution would score higher about 24% of the time.
- **Within-group variation dwarfs between-group variation.** The spread within either curve (±2 SD ≈ 60 points) is four times the distance between the means. Knowing which curve someone was drawn from tells you very little about their score.
- **Tails diverge proportionally more.** Above 130, the modeled rates would be ~2.3% vs ~0.1% — a feature of normal tails generally, and the part of such graphs most often over-interpreted.

## Important caveats about the content

**The graph shows a measured gap, not its cause.** A difference in test score averages between socially defined groups is an observation about test performance. It carries no information about *why* — nothing in this chart distinguishes genetic, environmental, educational, economic, health, or test-related explanations. The visual symmetry of two tidy bell curves can create a misleading impression of a fixed, natural, biological fact.

**The numbers are dated and the gap has narrowed.** These 1994 figures don't reflect subsequent convergence. Analyses of large US test batteries (e.g., Dickens & Flynn, 2006) find the gap shrank by several points over recent decades — which a purely fixed trait could not easily do.

**The Flynn effect undercuts the framing.** Raw IQ scores rose roughly 3 points per decade across the 20th century in many countries, meaning environmental change moved whole populations by *more* than 15 points within two generations. Whatever produces such shifts can plainly produce gaps of this size.

**"Race" here is a social classification.** The curves are defined by self-reported or administratively assigned census categories, which don't correspond to discrete biological populations. The grouping variable is a social one, so the comparison is between social categories with different histories of schooling, segregation, wealth, nutrition, and exposure to lead and other stressors.

**The hereditarian reading is not a scientific consensus.** The APA's 1996 task force report (*Intelligence: Knowns and Unknowns*), convened partly in response to *The Bell Curve*, concluded there was no adequate explanation for the gap and no direct evidence for a genetic one. That remains contested terrain; admixture studies have not found the associations a genetic account would predict.

## Methodological critiques of the figure itself

- It plots a model, not measurements: no sample, no sample sizes, no confidence intervals, no source data.
- Equal SDs are assumed rather than estimated (reported SDs typically differ somewhat between groups).
- The y-axis is unlabeled "relative frequency," so the curves aren't tied to any population counts.
- Smooth normal curves imply precision and permanence that the underlying estimates don't have.

**Bottom line:** the plot is a stylized restatement of one claim from a 1994 book — a one-SD mean difference with heavy overlap. It's best read as a statement about *measured test scores in a particular era*, not about innate ability, and certainly not as a basis for inferring anything about any individual.

# Interpreting the Plot

## What's literally shown

Two normal (bell-shaped) curves, each with standard deviation 15, centered at 100 and 85 respectively — a one-standard-deviation gap. The vertical dashed lines mark the means. The curves overlap substantially: roughly 70% of the area is shared, and a large fraction of each distribution falls within the range of the other. A randomly chosen person from the lower-mean group would score higher than a randomly chosen person from the higher-mean group about 24% of the time.

## Important context the plot omits

**Where the numbers come from.** The 85/100 figures are from Herrnstein and Murray's *The Bell Curve* (1994), which synthesized U.S. test data from the 1970s–80s. The book was heavily criticized — by the APA's own task force, by statisticians, and by many of the researchers whose data it used — for its interpretive leaps, not primarily for the raw descriptive numbers.

**The gap has narrowed.** Analyses of nationally representative datasets (NAEP, NLSY, standardization samples) find the Black–White test score gap shrank by roughly a third to a half between the 1970s and 2000s. A chart presenting 1994-era figures as current is out of date.

**"Race" here is a social category, not a biological one.** Genetic variation within these groups vastly exceeds variation between them, and the groups are defined by U.S. social classification, not genetic clustering.

**The plot shows a difference; it says nothing about cause.** This is the crucial point. Group mean differences in test scores are well documented and consistent with many causal stories: differences in schooling quality, family wealth (the racial wealth gap is roughly 10:1, far larger than the income gap), lead and other environmental exposures, health care access, test familiarity, stereotype effects, and historical discrimination compounding across generations. The Flynn effect — IQ scores rising ~3 points per decade worldwide — demonstrates that environmental factors can move population means by more than this gap within a single generation. Heritability *within* a group also tells you nothing about the causes of differences *between* groups, a point Richard Lewontin made with a well-known thought experiment about genetically identical seeds grown in rich versus poor soil.

**What IQ measures is itself contested.** IQ predicts some outcomes reasonably well and is stable within individuals, but it captures a particular slice of cognitive performance shaped by the testing context and prior exposure to the kinds of tasks tested.

## Rhetorically

Charts like this one are frequently deployed to imply innate group differences, with the visual authority of a clean statistical graphic doing work the underlying evidence doesn't support. Two features of this specific chart are worth noting: the title attributes the means to a single contested 1994 source without caveat, and it presents nothing about measurement error, sampling, time trends, or confounding. If you encountered this image somewhere, the source and surrounding argument matter at least as much as the curves.

The honest summary: these distributions reflect a real, measured, and shrinking difference in average test performance between socially defined groups in a specific historical context — and the plot provides no evidence whatsoever about why.

# Interpreting This Plot

## What's Shown
This line graph displays **average annual global temperature in Fahrenheit from 1880 to 2015**. The orange line hovers steadily around 56–58°F across the entire 135-year span, appearing almost perfectly flat.

## The Key Issue: Misleading Axis Scaling

The apparent "flatness" here is an artifact of the chart design, not the data. Notice:

- **The y-axis spans -10°F to 110°F** — a 120-degree range
- **The actual data varies by only ~2–3°F** over the full period
- That real variation occupies roughly **2% of the vertical space**, making it visually invisible

This is a classic example of how axis choice can shape (or distort) interpretation. A chart like this is sometimes used to argue that global warming is negligible — but the technique would work equally well to "disprove" a human fever, since the difference between 98.6°F and 104°F would also vanish on a 120-degree scale.

## Why Small Numbers Matter Here

Global average temperature is an aggregate of the entire planet's surface. The difference between today's climate and the **last ice age** — when ice sheets covered much of North America — is only about **7–13°F** in global average terms. So a 2°F shift is a substantial climatic change, not a rounding error.

## A Better Visualization Would:

1. **Scale the y-axis to the data range** (e.g., 55–59°F), letting the trend become legible
2. **Use temperature anomalies** (departures from a baseline average) rather than absolute values — the standard approach in climate science
3. **Add a trend line or smoothing** to distinguish year-to-year noise from long-term direction

## What the Data Actually Shows

Even in this compressed view, you can detect a faint rise on the right side of the chart — slightly lower values around 1900–1910, and a modest upward drift after about 1980. Properly scaled, this data shows roughly **2°F (1.1°C) of warming since 1880**, with most of it occurring after 1975.

**Bottom line:** The plot is technically accurate but rhetorically misleading. Always check the axis range before concluding a trend is flat.

Visually it looks almost flat, but that is mostly the scale. The y-axis runs from −10 to 110, so a real rise of roughly 1–2°F is compressed into a thin band and is hard to see. On a narrower axis centered on the data (for example about 55–60°F), the same series would show a clearer upward trend, especially after the mid-20th century.

## What the chart literally shows

Two idealized normal (Gaussian) curves, each with SD = 15, with means placed 15 points apart — 100 and 85. That's it. There's no data behind it: these are textbook bell curves drawn from two parameters, not histograms of measured scores.

**Implications of a one-SD separation:**

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Effect size (Cohen's d) | 1.0 |
| Overlap of the two distributions | ~62% |
| Share of the lower-mean curve above 100 | ~16% |
| Share of the higher-mean curve above 85 | ~84% |
| P(random draw from orange > random draw from blue) | ~24% |

Two features are worth noting because they're easy to misread:

1. **The overlap dominates.** The distributions are far more alike than different. Pick one person from each curve at random and the orange draw is higher roughly one time in four. Group membership is a very weak predictor of any individual's score — variance *within* each curve swamps the distance *between* them.
2. **Tails diverge sharply.** Above 130, the blue curve has ~2.3% and the orange ~0.13% — an ~18:1 ratio. Small mean shifts produce large ratio differences at the extremes, which is where this kind of chart is often used rhetorically.

## What the chart doesn't show, and why that matters

**The numbers are a snapshot being presented as a constant.** The 15-point figure comes from mid-20th-century US test data. By the 2000s the Black–White gap on standardized measures had narrowed to roughly 9–12 points (Dickens & Flynn 2006; NAEP trends). Over the same era the Flynn effect raised raw scores ~3 points per decade across all groups — meaning the difference between a 1950s cohort and a 1990s cohort is *larger* than the gap this chart draws. A quantity that moves that much over decades is not a fixed property of anything.

**A score gap is an observation; its cause is a separate question.** *The Bell Curve* (Herrnstein & Murray, 1994) is cited here, and its contested claim was not that the gap exists but that it is substantially genetic. The APA's response task force (Neisser et al., 1996) concluded there was no adequate explanation for the gap, genetic or otherwise. Candidate environmental contributors — school quality, segregation, parental wealth (not just income), childhood lead exposure, nutrition, test familiarity — are large, confounded with each other, and historically hard to disentangle.

**Within-group heritability does not license between-group inference.** This is the standard statistical error here. Plant genetically identical seeds in rich and poor soil: height is highly heritable within each plot and the difference between plots is entirely environmental. High heritability inside a group tells you nothing about the source of a difference between groups.

**"Race" is doing unstated work.** These are US social-census categories, not genetically discrete populations; most human genetic variation lies within such groupings rather than between them. The curves also assume each category is internally homogeneous enough to be a single Gaussian, which is an assumption, not a finding.

**The visual design asserts more precision than exists.** Smooth curves and dashed mean lines convey exactness. Missing: data source, sample, year, confidence intervals, and any indication that both parameters are estimates that have shifted over time.

## Bottom line

As a math exercise, it correctly renders two normal distributions one SD apart and illustrates that such a shift produces large overlap but lopsided tails. As an empirical claim, it presents a historical, era-specific, environment-sensitive average as if it were a stable fact, attaches it to a causal interpretation the chart itself cannot support, and uses group means in a way that says almost nothing about any individual.

# What the plot shows

Two normal distributions of IQ scores with equal standard deviations (15), centered at 100 and 85 — a one-standard-deviation gap. This is the familiar visual from *The Bell Curve* (Herrnstein & Murray, 1994), which plotted average test-score differences between self-identified racial groups in the United States.

Mechanically, the figure says: the curves overlap heavily (roughly 70% overlap), both have the same spread, and the variation *within* each group is far larger than the distance *between* the two means. Any given person could come from either distribution; knowing group membership tells you very little about an individual.

# What the plot does not show

The graphic is purely descriptive and carries no causal information, yet it is routinely read as though it does. Several things worth flagging:

**The numbers are dated and the gap has narrowed.** The ~15-point figure came from mid-20th-century test data. Analyses of NAEP, AFQT, and other standardized datasets show the Black–White gap shrinking substantially over recent decades — roughly a third or more on some measures. A static curve hides that trajectory.

**Group means say nothing about causes.** Test scores respond strongly to environment: nutrition, lead exposure, school quality, family wealth, neighborhood segregation, prenatal care, and test familiarity all move scores. The Flynn effect — population-wide IQ gains of roughly 3 points per decade through the 20th century — is itself evidence of how much environment can shift scores across a span far shorter than any genetic change could explain. Within-group heritability also does not license inferences about between-group differences; this is a well-known statistical error (Lewontin's seed-in-different-soil illustration).

**"Race" is not a biological variable here.** The groupings are social and self-reported categories. Human genetic variation is overwhelmingly continuous and within-population, so the x-axis labels don't correspond to discrete biological populations.

**Scientific reception.** *The Bell Curve*'s hereditarian interpretation of these gaps was heavily criticized on methodological grounds — selective citation, inadequate controls for socioeconomic status, and reliance on sources later shown to be problematic. The APA's 1996 task force report ("Intelligence: Knowns and Unknowns") concluded there was no adequate explanation for the gap and no direct evidence for a genetic one.

# Bottom line

As a statistical object, the figure illustrates two overlapping normal curves separated by one SD. As a claim about the world, it presents outdated numbers, implies a causal story it cannot support, and invites inferences about individuals that the overlap itself contradicts. If you encountered this chart somewhere, it's worth asking what argument it was being used to make.

The figure shows two overlapping normal curves of IQ scores, both with a standard deviation of 15. The blue curve is labeled White with a mean of 100; the orange curve is labeled Black with a mean of 85. Vertical dashed lines mark those means. The title attributes those means to *The Bell Curve* (1994).

What the drawing itself implies, if those parameters are taken as given:

- The curves are the same shape and width; only the location differs, by one standard deviation (15 points).
- They overlap substantially. A large share of each distribution falls in the same score range, so group membership does not determine an individual’s score.
- Because the Black mean is set one SD lower, more of that curve lies below common cutoffs (for example 70 or 85) and less of it lies above high cutoffs (for example 115 or 130). That is a mathematical consequence of shifting a normal curve, not an independent finding shown by the plot.
- The y-axis is relative frequency, not a count of people, so the figure says nothing about population size.

Caveats that the figure does not show:

- These are modeled normals, not raw data. Real score distributions are only approximately normal, and standard deviations are not always identical across groups.
- The 15-point gap is a contested summary from older literature, not a fixed biological constant. Measured Black–White gaps in the U.S. have varied by test, cohort, age, and era, and have narrowed on some assessments.
- A mean difference, even if accurately measured, does not identify a cause. Environment, schooling, socioeconomic conditions, health, and properties of the tests themselves are all part of the debate; the plot cannot separate them.
- Within-group spread (SD = 15) is large relative to the between-group shift drawn here, so the overlap—not the peaks—is the more important visual fact for any individual comparison.

## What the plot literally shows

Two idealized normal curves — not raw data — drawn with a common standard deviation of 15 and means set 15 points apart (100 and 85). Everything in the figure follows mechanically from those three numbers:

- **The separation is exactly 1 SD** (Cohen's *d* = 1.0).
- **The curves overlap heavily.** The overlapping area is about 62% of each distribution.
- Roughly **16% of the lower-mean distribution lies above the higher-mean group's average**, and about 16% of the higher-mean group falls below the lower group's average.
- **Within-group variation dwarfs the between-group difference.** In a pooled sample, group membership would account for only something on the order of 10% of the variance in scores — meaning an individual's group tells you very little about that individual's score.

That last point is the single most important thing the picture conveys, and it's easy to miss: the shaded gray region is most of the plot.

## What the plot does *not* show

**It isn't data.** These are smooth Gaussians generated from two parameters. Real score distributions are not perfectly normal, not equal in variance, and the means cited come from particular test batteries and particular samples from decades ago.

**The means aren't fixed constants.** Average test scores rose roughly 3 points per decade across the 20th century (the Flynn effect) — larger than this entire gap within two generations. The Black–White gap itself narrowed substantially from the 1970s through the 2000s, by roughly a third to a half in some cohort analyses (Dickens & Flynn 2006; NAEP trend data). A static two-curve picture hides all of this.

**It contains no causal information whatsoever.** A difference in group means is compatible with environmental causes, measurement artifacts, sampling issues, or any combination. The plot cannot distinguish among them, and labeling the axis "Race" rather than "test score by sampled group" invites a causal reading the geometry doesn't support.

## Context on the source

*The Bell Curve* (Herrnstein & Murray, 1994) reported this gap and suggested a partly genetic explanation. That inference was the most criticized part of the book. The APA's expert task force response, *Intelligence: Knowns and Unknowns* (Neisser et al., 1996), concluded that the gap was real in the data but that **there was no adequate explanation for it and no direct evidence supporting a genetic one.** That remains the mainstream position; subsequent genomic work (e.g., on polygenic scores and ancestry) has not supplied such evidence, and polygenic scores for educational attainment are known to lose predictive validity across ancestry groups for technical reasons.

The key statistical point is Lewontin's: **heritability within a group says nothing about the cause of differences between groups.** Genetically identical seed stock grown in rich versus poor soil shows high within-plot heritability of height and a purely environmental between-plot difference. Candidate environmental confounds here are substantial and documented — differences in school quality and funding, family wealth (far larger than income gaps), residential segregation, childhood lead exposure, prenatal and nutritional health, and test familiarity.

## Bottom line

As a graphic, it accurately renders two normal distributions one SD apart and honestly displays their large overlap. As an argument, it's a chart that presents a contested, time-varying, environmentally confounded empirical finding as though it were a clean parameter of nature — and the category on the legend is a social classification, not a biological one.

The Flynn effect (population IQ gains of ~3 points per decade, larger than the entire gap shown here across a few generations) demonstrates that these distributions are not fixed.
- **Real distributions.** Actual score distributions aren't perfectly normal, and SDs are not identical across groups.
- **The meaning of the grouping variable.** "White" and "Black" are social/census categories, not genetically discrete populations; human genetic variation is overwhelmingly within such categories rather than between them.

## Bottom line

As a statistical object, this is a textbook illustration of two normal distributions separated by one SD, with the standard lesson that **a one-SD mean difference produces heavy overlap and poor individual-level discrimination, while producing large ratios in the extreme tails**. As a claim about the world, it's a dated, decontextualized summary statistic presented in a way that visually foregrounds a group difference while omitting the sampling, temporal, and causal caveats needed to interpret it.

# Interpreting This Plot

## What's Shown

This line graph displays **average annual global temperature in Fahrenheit from 1880 to 2015**. The y-axis spans from roughly -10°F to 110°F, while the x-axis covers 135 years in decade increments.

## The Apparent Message

At first glance, the orange line appears **almost perfectly flat**, hovering around 57-58°F across the entire period. The visual impression is that global temperature has been essentially constant for over a century.

## Why This Is Misleading

This chart is a classic example of how **axis scaling can distort interpretation**:

- **The y-axis range is wildly inappropriate.** Global average temperature has varied by only about 2°F (roughly 1.1°C) over this period. Plotting that variation on a 120-degree scale compresses the real signal into near-invisibility.
- **The actual trend is real and significant.** A ~1.1°C rise represents a substantial climate shift with major consequences — but it's rendered as a nearly imperceptible wiggle here.
- **Looking closely**, you *can* see a slight dip around 1910, a modest rise through the 1940s, a plateau mid-century, and a more pronounced upward slope after about 1980 — the line does sit noticeably higher at the right edge than the left.

## The Lesson

Had the y-axis been scaled to the data's actual range (say, 56°F–59°F), the warming trend — especially the sharp acceleration after 1970 — would be dramatically visible. 

This graph demonstrates that **a technically accurate chart can still communicate a false impression**. Choosing an axis range that dwarfs the variable's natural variation is a common rhetorical technique used to make meaningful changes look trivial. Good practice is to scale axes to the data's relevant range, and to disclose when a scale has been chosen for effect.

The chart shows average annual global temperature from 1880 to 2015 as a nearly flat orange line around the mid-to-upper 50s °F, with only a slight rise toward the right. On this scale the change looks negligible.

That impression is mostly an artifact of the y-axis, which runs from about −10 to 110 °F. Real variation over this period is only on the order of 1–2 °F, so it is compressed into a thin band and the warming trend is visually minimized. A narrower axis around the data range would make the same rise much clearer.

## What the plot literally shows

Two normal (Gaussian) curves, each with SD = 15, centered at 100 and 85. This is a *stylized model*, not raw data — someone has drawn idealized bell curves from two summary statistics (a mean and an SD) rather than plotting actual score histograms. The dashed vertical lines mark the two means; the shaded regions are the areas under each curve.

The gap is 15 points = 1.0 SD, which is the figure popularized by Herrnstein and Murray's *The Bell Curve* (1994), drawing on US test data from roughly the 1960s–1980s.

## What the geometry implies

A few quantities are worth reading off a picture like this, because they're routinely misread:

- **The distributions overlap heavily.** For d = 1.0, the overlap coefficient is about 62%. The large gray region dominates the figure.
- **A randomly chosen person from the lower-mean group scores higher than a randomly chosen person from the higher-mean group about 24% of the time.** Group membership is a weak predictor at the individual level.
- **Variation within groups dwarfs variation between them.** Group membership accounts for roughly 20% of the variance in this model; ~80% sits inside the groups. Knowing someone's group tells you very little about their score.
- **Tail effects are amplified.** Because the curves are thin at the extremes, a 1 SD shift produces large *ratio* differences above, say, 130 — which is why such plots are often deployed in arguments about elite selection, even though they say almost nothing about any individual.

## Important caveats about the content

**The plot describes test scores, not causes.** A difference in group means on a test is a measurement, not an explanation. The visualization is causally silent, but it's typically presented in contexts that imply a genetic interpretation. That implication isn't supported by the data shown.

**Heritability within groups doesn't license inferences between groups.** This is the single most common error in this area. Height in a well-fed population is highly heritable, yet a mean height gap between two populations can be entirely nutritional (Lewontin's seed-in-different-soils analogy). Within-group heritability places essentially no constraint on the cause of a between-group difference.

**The numbers are dated and the gap has narrowed.** Dickens and Flynn (2006) and subsequent work found convergence of roughly 4–7 points over the late 20th century. Contemporary estimates are generally below 1 SD. A static plot hides this trend — and a gap that moves on a generational timescale is hard to attribute to genetics.

**The Flynn effect undercuts the framing.** Raw IQ scores rose ~3 points per decade across the 20th century in many countries — a shift larger than the gap depicted here, over a period too short for genetic change. This demonstrates that environments can move population means by more than 15 points.

**Confounds are massive and not independent.** The groups being compared differ systematically in income, wealth, school quality, segregation, lead exposure, healthcare access, and the legacy of legally enforced discrimination. These aren't nuisance variables to be statistically controlled away; several are plausibly on the causal path.

**Expert consensus is that the cause is unresolved.** The APA's task force report (Neisser et al., 1996) concluded there was no adequate explanation for the gap and explicitly found no direct evidence for a genetic one. Subsequent genomic work has not changed that; polygenic scores for educational attainment transfer poorly across ancestry groups for technical reasons (differences in linkage disequilibrium and allele frequencies), making them unsuitable for cross-group comparisons.

**"Race" isn't a clean biological variable.** The categories used here are social and administrative, with substantial internal genetic heterogeneity and admixture. Treating them as two discrete populations with crisp parameters is a modeling choice that obscures this.

## Bottom line

As a piece of data visualization, it's an accurate rendering of two normal distributions 1 SD apart — and its most striking visual feature is actually the *overlap*. As an argument, it's incomplete: it presents a dated, group-level descriptive statistic in a format that invites causal and individual-level inferences the underlying data can't support.

# Decomposition of the Gender Wage Gap, 2010

## What the chart shows

This horizontal bar chart breaks down the total gender wage gap into the fractions attributable to different labor-market variables, based on Blau and Kahn (2017). Bars extend right (positive contributions, widening the gap) or left (negative contributions, narrowing the gap) from a 0% baseline.

## The values, ranked

| Factor | Share of gap |
|---|---|
| Unexplained | 38% |
| Occupation | 32.9% |
| Industry | 17.6% |
| Experience | 14.1% |
| Race | 4.3% |
| Region | 0.3% |
| Unionization | −1.3% |
| Education | −5.9% |

## Key takeaways

**1. The largest single component is "unexplained."** At 38%, the residual left after accounting for all measured factors is the biggest piece. This is often interpreted as discrimination, though the chart's note cautions it may also capture unobserved differences in productivity.

**2. Occupational and industrial segregation together dominate the explained portion.** Occupation (32.9%) plus industry (17.6%) account for roughly half the total gap — meaning that *where* women work (lawyer vs. teacher; finance vs. healthcare) matters more than any other measurable characteristic.

**3. Experience still matters, but less.** Differences in years of labor-market experience explain 14.1%, reflecting the lingering effect of career interruptions.

**4. Education actually works in women's favor.** The −5.9% figure means that if education were the only factor, women would out-earn men — women's educational attainment now exceeds men's, so this variable *shrinks* rather than widens the gap. Unionization similarly contributes a small negative (−1.3%).

**5. Geography is essentially irrelevant.** Region contributes just 0.3%.

## Important caveats

The source note stresses these are estimates and the boundaries between factors are blurry. Crucially, the categories are not cleanly independent: discrimination may itself drive women into lower-paying occupations, so the "occupation" share partly embeds discriminatory processes. Conversely, the "unexplained" share isn't purely discrimination. The decomposition is a useful accounting exercise, not a clean causal attribution.

## What the figure shows

Two idealized normal (Gaussian) curves, not actual data — they're generated from two parameters each:

- **Blue:** mean 100, SD 15
- **Orange:** mean 85, SD 15

The 15-point gap equals exactly one standard deviation, so the effect size is **Cohen's d = 1.0**. The dashed vertical lines mark the two means. Everything else in the picture follows mechanically from those four numbers.

## Statistical implications of a d = 1 gap

- **Overlap is large.** The two distributions share roughly 62% of their area. Within-group variation is much larger than the between-group difference.
- **Group membership predicts little about an individual.** Knowing which curve someone was drawn from explains about 20% of the variance in scores. Roughly 16% of the orange distribution scores above the blue mean, and 16% of the blue distribution scores below the orange mean.
- **Tails amplify.** At a cutoff of 130, ~2.3% of blue vs. ~0.1% of orange qualify — a ~17-fold ratio. Small mean shifts in normal distributions produce large ratios far from center, which is why selective thresholds (gifted programs, elite admissions, high-cutoff job tests) show disparities far bigger than the mean gap suggests.

## Important interpretive caveats

**This is a model, not evidence.** The curves are drawn from assumed parameters. Nothing here is a measurement, a sample, or a test of any hypothesis. A plot like this can only restate assumptions more vividly.

**The plot is silent on causation.** Average score differences on IQ tests between US racial groups have been measured repeatedly and are not in dispute as *measurements*. What the measurements mean is heavily disputed. Candidate explanations include differences in schooling quality and funding, family wealth (the Black–white wealth gap is far larger than the income gap), neighborhood segregation, lead and other environmental exposures, prenatal and childhood health care, test familiarity and stereotype effects, and historical discrimination compounding across generations. The Bell Curve's suggestion of a partly genetic basis was contested at publication and remains a minority position; the APA's 1996 task force concluded there was no adequate explanation for the gap and no direct evidence for a genetic one. Group differences in a trait can be entirely environmental even when the trait is highly heritable *within* groups — this is a well-known inferential trap.

**The numbers are dated and the gap is not fixed.** The 85 figure reflects data available before 1994. Analyses of NAEP and other large assessments show the gap narrowing substantially over the 20th century, to roughly 0.6–0.8 SD in more recent cohorts. A static plot implies a permanence the data don't support. Relatedly, the Flynn effect — population-wide gains of roughly 3 points per decade — means whole populations have shifted by more than this gap within a few generations, which is hard to square with a fixed biological ceiling.

**"Race" is doing unexamined work.** The categories here are US social/administrative classifications with enormous genetic heterogeneity within each and considerable ancestry overlap between them. They are not natural kinds that would be expected to partition a biological trait cleanly.

## Bottom line

As a statistics exercise, the plot correctly illustrates how two normal distributions separated by one SD behave — especially the counterintuitive combination of *heavy overlap in the middle* and *large ratios in the tails*. As a claim about the world, it presents one contested interpretation of dated data as a clean mathematical fact, which is exactly the rhetorical effect that makes this kind of chart popular in arguments it can't actually settle.
